title: 团队选了另一个方案，怎样表达保留意见又继续配合？
topic: 表达异议后承诺执行最终方案

source.title: Jeff Bezos’ 2016 Letter to Amazon Shareholders
source.section: Jeff Bezos’ 2016 Letter to Amazon Shareholders
source.type: 公开股东信：团队决策实践
source.context: Amazon CEO 股东信中对团队决策的公开介绍
source.author: Jeff Bezos
paragraphs: Third, use the phrase “disagree and commit.” This phrase will save a lot of time. If you have conviction on a particular direction even though there’s no consensus, it’s helpful to say, “Look, I know we disagree on this but will you gamble with me on it? Disagree and commit?” By the time you’re at this point, no one can know the answer for sure, and you’ll probably get a quick yes.

This isn’t one way. If you’re the boss, you should do this too. I disagree and commit all the time. We recently greenlit a particular Amazon Studios original. I told the team my view: debatable whether it would be interesting enough, complicated to produce, the business terms aren’t that good, and we have lots of other opportunities. They had a completely different opinion and wanted to go ahead. I wrote back right away with “I disagree and commit and hope it becomes the most watched thing we’ve ever made.” Consider how much slower this decision cycle would have been if the team had actually had to convince me rather than simply get my commitment.

Note what this example is not: it’s not me thinking to myself “well, these guys are wrong and missing the point, but this isn’t worth me chasing.” It’s a genuine disagreement of opinion, a candid expression of my view, a chance for the team to weigh my view, and a quick, sincere commitment to go their way. And given that this team has already brought home 11 Emmys, 6 Golden Globes, and 3 Oscars, I’m just glad they let me in the room at all!
translations: 第三，使用“不同意，但承诺执行”这句话。这能节省很多时间。如果你对某个方向很有信心，但团队还没有达成一致，可以这样说：“我知道我们在这件事上意见不同，但你愿意和我一起赌一把吗？不同意，但承诺执行？”到了这个阶段，谁也无法确定答案，你通常会很快得到肯定答复。

这并非只适用于一种角色。如果你是老板，也应该这么做。我经常在表达不同意见后承诺执行。最近我们批准了一部 Amazon Studios 原创作品。我把看法告诉团队：这部作品是否足够有趣还值得商榷，制作起来很复杂，商业条件也不太好，而且我们还有很多其他机会。团队的看法完全不同，希望继续推进。我立刻回复：“我不同意，但我承诺执行；希望它成为我们做过的播放量最高的作品。”如果团队必须先说服我，而不是只需要得到我的承诺，想想整个决策过程会慢多少。
注意，这个例子不是说我心里想“他们错了，没抓住重点，但这事不值得我继续追究”。这是观点上的真实分歧，是坦率表达我的看法，让团队有机会权衡我的意见，然后我迅速、真诚地承诺按他们的决定推进。考虑到这个团队已经拿下 11 项艾美奖、6 项金球奖和 3 项奥斯卡奖，我很庆幸他们还让我参与讨论！
fullTextParagraphs: “Jeff, what does Day 2 look like?”

That’s a question I just got at our most recent all-hands meeting. I’ve been reminding people that it’s Day 1 for a couple of decades. I work in an Amazon building named Day 1, and when I moved buildings, I took the name with me. I spend time thinking about this topic.
“Day 2 is stasis. Followed by irrelevance. Followed by excruciating, painful decline. Followed by death. And that is why it is always Day 1.”
To be sure, this kind of decline would happen in extreme slow motion. An established company might harvest Day 2 for decades, but the final result would still come.
I’m interested in the question, how do you fend off Day 2? What are the techniques and tactics? How do you keep the vitality of Day 1, even inside a large organization?

Such a question can’t have a simple answer. There will be many elements, multiple paths, and many traps. I don’t know the whole answer, but I may know bits of it. Here’s a starter pack of essentials for Day 1 defense: customer obsession, a skeptical view of proxies, the eager adoption of external trends, and high-velocity decision making.

There are many ways to center a business. You can be competitor focused, you can be product focused, you can be technology focused, you can be business model focused, and there are more. But in my view, obsessive customer focus is by far the most protective of Day 1 vitality.

Why? There are many advantages to a customer-centric approach, but here’s the big one: customers are always beautifully, wonderfully dissatisfied, even when they report being happy and business is great. Even when they don’t yet know it, customers want something better, and your desire to delight customers will drive you to invent on their behalf. No customer ever asked Amazon to create the Prime membership program, but it sure turns out they wanted it, and I could give you many such examples.

Staying in Day 1 requires you to experiment patiently, accept failures, plant seeds, protect saplings, and double down when you see customer delight. A customer-obsessed culture best creates the conditions where all of that can happen.
As companies get larger and more complex, there’s a tendency to manage to proxies. This comes in many shapes and sizes, and it’s dangerous, subtle, and very Day 2.

A common example is process as proxy. Good process serves you so you can serve customers. But if you’re not watchful, the process can become the thing. This can happen very easily in large organizations. The process becomes the proxy for the result you want. You stop looking at outcomes and just make sure you’re doing the process right. Gulp. It’s not that rare to hear a junior leader defend a bad outcome with something like, “Well, we followed the process.” A more experienced leader will use it as an opportunity to investigate and improve the process. The process is not the thing. It’s always worth asking, do we own the process or does the process own us? In a Day 2 company, you might find it’s the second.

Another example: market research and customer surveys can become proxies for customers – something that’s especially dangerous when you’re inventing and designing products. “Fifty-five percent of beta testers report being satisfied with this feature. That is up from 47% in the first survey.” That’s hard to interpret and could unintentionally mislead.

Good inventors and designers deeply understand their customer. They spend tremendous energy developing that intuition. They study and understand many anecdotes rather than only the averages you’ll find on surveys. They live with the design.

I’m not against beta testing or surveys. But you, the product or service owner, must understand the customer, have a vision, and love the offering. Then, beta testing and research can help you find your blind spots. A remarkable customer experience starts with heart, intuition, curiosity, play, guts, taste. You won’t find any of it in a survey.
The outside world can push you into Day 2 if you won’t or can’t embrace powerful trends quickly. If you fight them, you’re probably fighting the future. Embrace them and you have a tailwind.

These big trends are not that hard to spot (they get talked and written about a lot), but they can be strangely hard for large organizations to embrace. We’re in the middle of an obvious one right now: machine learning and artificial intelligence.

Over the past decades computers have broadly automated tasks that programmers could describe with clear rules and algorithms. Modern machine learning techniques now allow us to do the same for tasks where describing the precise rules is much harder.

At Amazon, we’ve been engaged in the practical application of machine learning for many years now. Some of this work is highly visible: our autonomous Prime Air delivery drones; the Amazon Go convenience store that uses machine vision to eliminate checkout lines; and Alexa,1 our cloud-based AI assistant. (We still struggle to keep Echo in stock, despite our best efforts. A high-quality problem, but a problem. We’re working on it.)

But much of what we do with machine learning happens beneath the surface. Machine learning drives our algorithms for demand forecasting, product search ranking, product and deals recommendations, merchandising placements, fraud detection, translations, and much more. Though less visible, much of the impact of machine learning will be of this type – quietly but meaningfully improving core operations.
Inside AWS, we’re excited to lower the costs and barriers to machine learning and AI so organizations of all sizes can take advantage of these advanced techniques.

Using our pre-packaged versions of popular deep learning frameworks running on P2 compute instances (optimized for this workload), customers are already developing powerful systems ranging everywhere from early disease detection to increasing crop yields. And we’ve also made Amazon’s higher level services available in a convenient form. Amazon Lex (what’s inside Alexa), Amazon Polly, and Amazon Rekognition remove the heavy lifting from natural language understanding, speech generation, and image analysis. They can be accessed with simple API calls – no machine learning expertise required. Watch this space. Much more to come.

Day 2 companies make high-quality decisions, but they make high-quality decisions slowly. To keep the energy and dynamism of Day 1, you have to somehow make high-quality, high-velocity decisions. Easy for start-ups and very challenging for large organizations. The senior team at Amazon is determined to keep our decision-making velocity high. Speed matters in business – plus a high-velocity decision making environment is more fun too. We don’t know all the answers, but here are some thoughts.

First, never use a one-size-fits-all decision-making process. Many decisions are reversible, two-way doors. Those decisions can use a light-weight process. For those, so what if you’re wrong? I wrote about this in more detail in last year’s letter.

Second, most decisions should probably be made with somewhere around 70% of the information you wish you had. If you wait for 90%, in most cases, you’re probably being slow. Plus, either way, you need to be good at quickly recognizing and correcting bad decisions. If you’re good at course correcting, being wrong may be less costly than you think, whereas being slow is going to be expensive for sure.

Third, use the phrase “disagree and commit.” This phrase will save a lot of time. If you have conviction on a particular direction even though there’s no consensus, it’s helpful to say, “Look, I know we disagree on this but will you gamble with me on it? Disagree and commit?” By the time you’re at this point, no one can know the answer for sure, and you’ll probably get a quick yes.

This isn’t one way. If you’re the boss, you should do this too. I disagree and commit all the time. We recently greenlit a particular Amazon Studios original. I told the team my view: debatable whether it would be interesting enough, complicated to produce, the business terms aren’t that good, and we have lots of other opportunities. They had a completely different opinion and wanted to go ahead. I wrote back right away with “I disagree and commit and hope it becomes the most watched thing we’ve ever made.” Consider how much slower this decision cycle would have been if the team had actually had to convince me rather than simply get my commitment.

Note what this example is not: it’s not me thinking to myself “well, these guys are wrong and missing the point, but this isn’t worth me chasing.” It’s a genuine disagreement of opinion, a candid expression of my view, a chance for the team to weigh my view, and a quick, sincere commitment to go their way. And given that this team has already brought home 11 Emmys, 6 Golden Globes, and 3 Oscars, I’m just glad they let me in the room at all!

Fourth, recognize true misalignment issues early and escalate them immediately. Sometimes teams have different objectives and fundamentally different views. They are not aligned. No amount of discussion, no number of meetings will resolve that deep misalignment. Without escalation, the default dispute resolution mechanism for this scenario is exhaustion. Whoever has more stamina carries the decision.

I’ve seen many examples of sincere misalignment at Amazon over the years. When we decided to invite third party sellers to compete directly against us on our own product detail pages – that was a big one. Many smart, well-intentioned Amazonians were simply not at all aligned with the direction. The big decision set up hundreds of smaller decisions, many of which needed to be escalated to the senior team.
“You’ve worn me down” is an awful decision-making process. It’s slow and de-energizing. Go for quick escalation instead – it’s better.

So, have you settled only for decision quality, or are you mindful of decision velocity too? Are the world’s trends tailwinds for you? Are you falling prey to proxies, or do they serve you? And most important of all, are you delighting customers? We can have the scope and capabilities of a large company and the spirit and heart of a small one. But we have to choose it.
A huge thank you to each and every customer for allowing us to serve you, to our shareowners for your support, and to Amazonians everywhere for your hard work, your ingenuity, and your passion.
As always, I attach a copy of our original 1997 letter. It remains Day 1.
Jeffrey P. BezosFounder and Chief Executive OfficerAmazon.com, Inc.
1 For something amusing, try asking, “Alexa, what is sixty factorial?”

notes.meaning: 表达分歧后，仍承诺支持团队最终决定。
notes.explain: disagree and commit 常用于充分讨论后的决策阶段。
notes.example: I still have concerns about the launch date, but I disagree and commit.

notes.phrase: I disagree and commit and hope it becomes the most watched thing we’ve ever made.
notes.meaning: 先表达顾虑，再明确承诺支持最终选择。
notes.explain: 这句话把不同意见和承诺执行放在同一句里。
notes.example: I disagree with the timing, but I’ll support the decision and update the launch plan.

notes.meaning: 真诚说明自己不同意，同时接受团队决定。
notes.explain: genuine 表示真实的；这里强调不是表面答应、实际不配合。
notes.example: I have a different view, but I’ll help the team make the decision work.

scenario.title: 模拟：团队选择了另一个发布方案
english: Your team has chosen to move a product launch to the following month.
You think the original date is still possible, but the decision owner has heard your reasons and made the call.
You acknowledge the decision, state your remaining concern briefly, and offer a concrete next step to support the plan.
chinese: 团队决定把产品发布推迟到下个月。
你认为仍有可能按原日期发布，但负责人听取意见后已经做出决定。
你确认最终决定，简短说明仍有的顾虑，并提出一项支持计划的具体行动。

firstAttempt.prompt: 你不同意团队选择的发布方案，但负责人已经做出决定。请用英文简短说明自己的顾虑，同时明确你会支持最终决定并配合下一步。
firstAttempt.sample: I know we disagree on the launch date. I still have concerns about moving the launch to next month, but I understand the decision. I’ll support the decision and update the launch checklist today.
firstAttempt.rationale: 说清保留意见，也让团队知道你会配合决定和下一步。

words.example: I have conviction that this option will work for our customers.
words.translation: 我坚信这个方案会对客户有效。
words.note: 用于表达自己有充分理由坚持某个方向。

words.example: I’ll commit to the plan and update the launch checklist.
words.translation: 我会支持这个计划，并更新上线清单。
words.note: commit to 后接名词或动名词。

words.example: I’d like to weigh in on the launch date before we decide.
words.translation: 在决定之前，我想对上线日期发表一下看法。
words.note: 常接 on + 讨论事项。

taskPhrases.meaning: 我知道我们在……上意见不同。
taskPhrases.example: I know we disagree on the launch date.
taskPhrases.translation: 我知道我们对上线日期意见不同。

taskPhrases.example: I still have concerns about moving the launch to next month.
taskPhrases.translation: 我对把上线时间推迟到下个月仍有些顾虑。

taskPhrases.example: I’ll support the decision and update the launch checklist today.
taskPhrases.translation: 我会支持这个决定，并在今天更新上线清单。

structure.original: I disagree and commit and hope it becomes the most watched thing we’ve ever made.
analysis: I disagree and commit：把表达不同意见与承诺执行放在一句中。
hope it becomes…：表达对结果的期待，不把结果说成确定。
structure.transfer: I disagree with the format, but I’ll support the team’s decision and update the deck today.

rewrite.good: I know we disagree on the launch date. I still have concerns about moving it to next month, but I’ll support the decision and update the launch checklist today.
rewrite.translation: 我知道我们对上线日期意见不同。我对把日期推迟到下个月仍有些顾虑，但我会支持这个决定，并在今天更新上线清单。
rewrite.pattern: I know we disagree on [issue]. I still have concerns about [option], but I’ll support the decision and [action].

cloze.prompt: I know we ______ on the launch date.
cloze.why: disagree on + 事项表示对某件事意见不同。

cloze.prompt: I still have ______ about moving it to next month.
cloze.why: have concerns about + 事项表示对某事有顾虑。

cloze.prompt: I’ll ______ the decision and update the checklist.
cloze.why: support the decision 表示支持最终决定。

dictation.label: 听写 1
dictation.text: Third, use the phrase “disagree and commit.”
dictation.why: 听清 disagree and commit 连续出现时的重音。

apply.prompt: 我们对发布日期意见不同，但我会支持最终决定。
apply.sample: We disagree on the launch date, but I’ll support the decision.

dictation.label: 听写 2
dictation.text: I disagree and commit and hope it becomes the most watched thing we’ve ever made.
dictation.why: 留意 I disagree and commit 后面接的希望表达。

apply.prompt: 我仍有顾虑，但会配合团队的最终决定。
apply.sample: I still have concerns, but I’ll support the team’s decision.

translationPractice.prompt: 我知道我们对上线日期意见不同。
translationPractice.answer: I know we disagree on the launch date.
translationPractice.why: 先明确分歧具体在哪件事上。

translationPractice.prompt: 我对把上线时间推迟到下个月仍有些顾虑。
translationPractice.answer: I still have concerns about moving the launch to next month.
translationPractice.why: 用 concerns about 说明仍未消除的顾虑。

translationPractice.prompt: 我会支持这个决定，并在今天更新上线清单。
translationPractice.answer: I’ll support the decision and update the launch checklist today.
translationPractice.why: 给出具体行动，表明会配合执行。

choice.prompt: 团队已经决定把客户培训推迟一周，你原本建议按期举行。哪句话既保留意见，也说明你会配合？
options: That is a bad decision. I will do what I want.
I still have concerns about the delay, but I understand the decision. I’ll update the customer materials today.
Fine. Don’t ask me for help.
choice.why: 第二条说出具体顾虑，也提出支持决定的行动。

output.prompt: 主管决定把市场报告改为简版，你原本建议保留详细分析。请用英文说明你仍担心客户会看不到关键依据，但会支持决定，并提出下一步。
output.sample: I still have concerns that the short version may leave out some important evidence, but I understand the decision. I’ll support the new format and add a link to the full analysis.
check: 提出配合执行的下一步
